stem.text: This question is about the hydroxides and carbonates of magnesium and barium.

stem.caption: Options A to D
head: the more soluble hydroxide
the carbonate with the greater thermal stability

explanation.text: Down Group 2 the hydroxides become more soluble, so Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> is more soluble than Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> is only sparingly soluble).

The carbonates become more thermally stable down the group. A small, highly charged cation such as Mg<sup>2+</sup> polarises the large carbonate ion more strongly, weakening its C–O bonds so that it decomposes to the oxide and CO<sub>2</sub> more easily. The larger Ba<sup>2+</sup> ion polarises it less, so BaCO<sub>3</sub> is the more stable carbonate.

optionAnalysis.text: Correct. Hydroxide solubility and carbonate thermal stability both increase down Group 2, so barium wins in both columns.
The carbonate is right, but Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> is the less soluble hydroxide.
The hydroxide is right, but MgCO<sub>3</sub> decomposes more easily than BaCO<sub>3</sub>.

reasoningChain: Hydroxide solubility increases down the group: Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> is more soluble.
Carbonate thermal stability increases down the group: BaCO<sub>3</sub> is more stable.

inferredMistakes.text: Mixing up the hydroxide trend with the sulfate trend, where solubility decreases down the group.
Thinking the smaller Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion holds the carbonate ion more firmly and so makes MgCO<sub>3</sub> more stable.
